Chapter overview

Study Sangam Literature through sources, the Three Sangams tradition, Tolkappiyam, Akam–Puram and Thinai conventions, Ettuthokai, Pattuppattu, major poets, metres, historical use and revision. Detailed political history remains in Chapter 3.

Sources & poeticsEttuthokaiPattuppattuEvidence & revision
Sangam Literature: Scope and Sources

The Sangam corpus is studied through literary works and corroborating inscriptional, archaeological, numismatic and foreign evidence.

Scope

Sangam literature broadly includes:

  • Tolkappiyam
  • Ettuthokai — Eight Anthologies
  • Pattuppattu — Ten Long Poems

Ettuthokai and Pattuppattu together are known as Pathinenmelkanakku, the Eighteen Major Works.

Detailed Sangam political history, rulers, battles and administration belong to Chapter 3. This chapter focuses on literary works, authors, patrons, classifications and distinctive factual associations.

Sources and Historical Value

Sangam literature must be read together with other categories of evidence.

  • Literary works — Tolkappiyam, Ettuthokai and Pattuppattu.
  • Inscriptions — Tamil-Brahmi records such as Mangulam, Jambai and Pugalur.
  • Archaeology — settlements, ports, craft centres and material remains from sites such as Keezhadi, Karur, Kodumanal, Korkai and Poompuhar.
  • Coins — Chera, Chola, Pandya and Roman coin finds.
  • Foreign accounts — Ashoka’s edicts, the Periplus, Pliny and Ptolemy.
  • Literary value — grammar, poetics, language, music and emotional conventions.
  • Historical value — rulers, ports, trade, occupations, social customs and warfare, subject to poetic exaggeration and chronological caution.

Detailed political history, battles and administration remain in Chapter 3: Sangam Age.

Three Sangams: Literary Tradition

The three-Sangams narrative is culturally important but belongs to a later commentary tradition rather than securely established chronology.

Meaning of Sangam

The word Sangam refers to an assembly or academy of poets and scholars.

The surviving Ettuthokai and Pattuppattu poems themselves do not use the expression “Sangam literature” as the name of their corpus.

The tradition of three Tamil Sangams is recorded in the later commentary on Iraiyanar Akapporul.

According to this tradition:

  • First Sangam — Then Madurai
  • Second Sangam — Kapatapuram
  • Third Sangam — present-day Madurai

The first two Sangams are said to have been destroyed by the sea.

The three-Sangam account is a traditional literary narrative and cannot be treated as a fully established historical chronology.

Tolkappiyam: Author, Structure and Divisions

Tolkappiyam is the oldest extant Tamil grammatical work and combines grammar with poetics and literary convention.

Tolkappiyam

Author: Tolkappiyar

Type: Grammar and poetics

Status: Oldest extant Tamil grammatical work

Tolkappiyam deals with:

  • Tamil sounds and letters
  • Words and grammatical forms
  • Sentence formation
  • Meaning and literary subject matter
  • Akam and Puram conventions
  • Poetic metres
  • Figures of speech
  • Social and literary traditions

Its exact date remains debated. It contains layers that may have developed over a long period.

Three Divisions of Tolkappiyam

Tolkappiyam contains three major divisions.

Ezhuttadikaram

Deals with:

  • Letters
  • Sounds
  • Pronunciation
  • Combination of letters
  • Phonological changes
Solladikaram

Deals with:

  • Words
  • Nouns
  • Verbs
  • Grammatical particles
  • Case relations
  • Word formation and usage
Poruladikaram

Deals with:

  • Akam poetry
  • Puram poetry
  • Thinai classification
  • Emotions and bodily expressions
  • Simile
  • Prosody
  • Literary conventions

Each of the three divisions contains nine Iyals, giving a total of 27 Iyals.

Akam and Puram Conventions

Akam organises private emotional experience, while Puram organises public action, ethics and named historical actors.

Akam and Puram
Akam Participants

The recurring literary roles include the hero, heroine, friend, foster mother and messenger. Personal names are generally avoided because the emotional situation, not individual biography, is central.

Concise Comparison
  • Akam — private emotional life; love, union, waiting, separation, quarrel, courtship and marriage.
  • Puram — public action; war, kingship, generosity, victory, death, heroism and ethics.
  • Akam usually avoids personal names; Puram frequently names rulers, chieftains, poets, places and battles.
Akam

Akam means the inner or private sphere.

It deals mainly with:

  • Love
  • Courtship
  • Union
  • Waiting
  • Separation
  • Lovers’ quarrels
  • Marriage

Personal names of the hero and heroine are generally avoided in Akam poetry.

Puram

Puram means the outer or public sphere.

It deals mainly with:

  • War
  • Kingship
  • Victory
  • Generosity
  • Public ethics
  • Death
  • Heroism
  • Poets and patrons

Named rulers, chiefs, poets, places and battles frequently appear in Puram poetry.

Thinai Classification

Thinai links landscape, emotion, deity, time, season, people and livelihood in Akam poetry.

Akam Thinai Associations
Kurinji

Landscape: Mountains

Theme: Union of lovers

Season: Cold or rainy season

Time: Midnight

Deity: Seyon or Murugan

Kuravar communities are associated with the hills; hunting, honey collection and millet cultivation were important occupations.

Mullai

Landscape: Forest and pastoral region

Theme: Patient waiting

Season: Rainy season

Time: Evening

Deity: Mayon or Thirumal

Ayar and Idaiyar communities are associated with pastoral life; cattle, sheep and goat rearing produced milk, curd, butter and ghee.

Marutham

Landscape: Agricultural plains

Theme: Domestic disagreement or infidelity

Time: Dawn

Deity: Vendan or Indra

Uzhavar and Vellalar are associated with settled agriculture; paddy and sugarcane were major crops.

Neithal

Landscape: Coast

Theme: Lament and anxious waiting

Time: Sunset

Deity: Varunan

Parathavar communities are associated with fishing, salt production, pearl diving and navigation.

Palai

Landscape: Arid or transformed dry land

Theme: Separation and dangerous journey

Season: Summer

Time: Midday

Deity: Korravai

Eyinar and Maravar appear in literary classification; hunting, cattle raids, warfare and long-distance travel are important associations.

Kaikkilai

One-sided or unreciprocated love.

Perunthinai

Improper, unsuitable or mismatched love.

The association of landscapes, emotions, seasons, occupations and deities is systematised in Tolkappiyam.

Muthalporul, Karupporul and Uripporul

These three categories explain how setting, landscape-linked features and human emotion work together in Akam poetry.

Three Elements of Akam Thinai

Tolkappiyam links landscape and time with the material features of a region and the human emotion expressed in the poem.

Muthalporul

Basic setting consisting of land and time.

Karupporul

Features associated with the landscape, such as deity, people, animals, plants, food and occupation.

Uripporul

The central human emotion or conduct associated with the Thinai.

These conventions are systematised in Tolkappiyam and employed throughout Akam literature.

Muthalporul provides the setting, Karupporul supplies the landscape-linked world, and Uripporul expresses the central human conduct or emotion.

Ettuthokai

The Eight Anthologies preserve five Akam collections, two Puram collections and one mixed devotional-musical anthology.

Eight Anthologies

The Ettuthokai consists of:

  • Natrinai
  • Kuruntokai
  • Ainkurunuru
  • Akananuru
  • Kalithokai
  • Purananuru
  • Pathitrupathu
  • Paripadal
Akam Anthologies
  • Natrinai
  • Kuruntokai
  • Ainkurunuru
  • Akananuru
  • Kalithokai
Puram Anthologies
  • Purananuru
  • Pathitrupathu
Akam and Puram Combined
  • Paripadal

The anthologies contain poems composed by numerous poets and later arranged into organised collections.

Natrinai

Meaning: Four hundred excellent Thinai poems

Number of poems: 400

Theme: Akam

Length: Generally 9–12 lines

Patron of compilation: Pandyan Pannadu Thanda Maran Valuthi

Compiler: Name unknown

The anthology contains poems attributed to 175 poets, while the authorship of several poems is unknown.

The invocation to Thirumal was composed by Bharatham Paadiya Perunthevanar.

Natrinai poems are longer than most Kuruntokai poems but shorter than Akananuru poems.

Kuruntokai

Meaning: Collection of short poems

Number of poems: 400

Theme: Akam

Length: Generally 4–8 lines

Compiler: Purikko

Poets: 205

The invocation to Murugan was composed by Bharatham Paadiya Perunthevanar.

Several poets are known by names derived from memorable expressions in their poems.

Examples include:

  • Aniladu Muntrilar
  • Kuppaikozhiyar
  • Vittakuthiraiyar

Kuruntokai is noted for presenting an entire emotional situation within a few lines.

Ainkurunuru

Meaning: Five hundred short poems

Number of poems: 500

Theme: Akam

Compiler: Pulathurai Mutriya Kudalur Kilar

Patron: Yanaikatsey Mantaran Cheral Irumporai

Each of the five landscapes contains 100 poems.

Authors by Thinai
  • Marutham — Orampogiyar
  • Neithal — Ammuvanar
  • Kurinji — Kapilar
  • Palai — Othalant aiyar
  • Mullai — Peyanar

The poems are arranged in the order:

Marutham → Neithal → Kurinji → Palai → Mullai

Each group of 100 poems is further divided into ten groups of ten.

The Tondippattu section follows the Antati pattern, where the end of one poem connects with the beginning of the next.

Poems 129 and 130 have not survived.

Akananuru

Other name: Nedunthokai

Number of poems: 400

Theme: Akam

Metre: Asiriyappa or Akaval

Patron: Pandyan Ukkirap Peruvazhuthi

Compiler: Madurai Uppurikudi Kizhar’s son Uruthirasanman

The poems generally contain between 13 and 31 lines.

Three Divisions
  • Kalittriyanai Nirai — Poems 1–120
  • Manimidai Pavalam — Poems 121–300
  • Nittilakkovai — Poems 301–400
Numerical Thinai Arrangement
  • Odd-numbered poems — Palai
  • Numbers ending in 2 or 8 — Kurinji
  • Numbers ending in 4 — Mullai
  • Numbers ending in 6 — Marutham
  • Numbers ending in 0 — Neithal

The invocation to Siva was composed by Bharatham Paadiya Perunthevanar.

Akananuru contains references to rulers, battles, marriage practices, Yavana ships and the pepper trade at Muchiri.

Kalithokai

Number of poems: 150, including the invocation

Theme: Akam

Metre: Kalippa

Compiler: Nallanthuvanar

Authors and Sections
  • Palaikkali — Perunkadungon — 35 poems
  • Kurinjikkali — Kapilar — 29 poems
  • Maruthakkali — Maruthan Ilanaganar — 35 poems
  • Mullaikkali — Cholan Nalluruthiran — 17 poems
  • Neithalkali — Nallanthuvanar — 33 poems

Kalithokai frequently uses dialogue and dramatic presentation.

It contains references to:

  • Eru Thazhuvuthal or bull embracing
  • Kaikkilai
  • Perunthinai
  • Ramayana and Mahabharata episodes
  • Madurai and the Vaigai

The opening invocation is addressed to Siva.

Purananuru

Meaning: Four hundred Puram poems

Theme: War, kingship, public life and ethics

Metre: Predominantly Akaval

Compiler: Unknown

Patron of compilation: Unknown

The collection was traditionally arranged as 400 poems.

Poems 267 and 268 are lost, and portions of several other poems are damaged.

The invocation to Siva was composed by Bharatham Paadiya Perunthevanar.

Purananuru is a major source for:

  • Chera, Chola and Pandya rulers
  • Minor chieftains
  • Battles
  • Hero stones
  • Warfare customs
  • Generosity
  • Poets and patrons
  • Death and mourning
  • Ethical ideas

It contains poems by more than 150 named poets.

Famous Purananuru Associations
  • Kaniyan Pungundranar — “Yadhum Oore Yaavarum Kelir” — Poem 192
  • Pisirandaiyar — friendship with Kopperuncholan
  • Avvaiyar — poems on Adiyaman Neduman Anji
  • Kapilar — poems on Vel Pari
  • Kovur Kilar — advice to Chola rulers
  • Okkur Masathiyar — heroic mother tradition
Pathitrupathu

Meaning: Ten groups of ten poems

Original number: 100 poems

Surviving number: 80 poems

Theme: Puram

Dynasty celebrated: Cheras

The first and tenth groups have been lost.

Each surviving group contains ten poems on one Chera ruler by one poet.

Surviving Decads
  • Second decad — Imayavaramban Neduncheralathan — Kumattur Kannanar
  • Third decad — Palyanai Sel Kelu Kuttuvan — Palai Kauthamanar
  • Fourth decad — Kalankay Kanni Narmudi Cheral — Kappiyatru Kappiyanar
  • Fifth decad — Kadal Pirakottiya Senguttuvan — Paranar
  • Sixth decad — Adu Kotpattu Cheralathan — Kakkaipadiniyar Nachellaiyar
  • Seventh decad — Selvak Kadungo Vazhiyathan — Kapilar
  • Eighth decad — Tagadur Erindha Peruncheral Irumporai — Arisil Kilar
  • Ninth decad — Ilancheral Irumporai — Perunkunrur Kilar

Each decad contains a Patikam, which gives details such as:

  • Ruler’s name and lineage
  • Poet’s name
  • Achievements of the ruler
  • Period of rule
  • Gifts given to the poet
  • Titles of the poems

The fourth decad is arranged in the Antati style.

Paripadal

Original number according to tradition: 70 poems

Surviving material: 22 complete poems, fragments and two poems preserved through Purathirattu

Theme: Akam, devotion and praise

Metre: Paripadal

The poems praise:

  • Thirumal
  • Murugan
  • Vaigai river
  • Madurai
  • Korravai in the original corpus

A distinctive feature of Paripadal is that each poem records:

  • Name of the poet
  • Name of the musician who set the tune
  • Name of the musical Pann

Thirteen poets and ten musical specialists are associated with the surviving collection.

Paripadal is the Sangam anthology most directly connected with organised music and devotional poetry.

Pattuppattu

The Ten Long Poems include Akam and Puram works, five Arruppadai poems, and major descriptions of patrons, cities, routes, ports and landscapes.

Ten Long Poems

The Pattuppattu consists of:

  • Tirumurukarruppatai
  • Porunararruppatai
  • Sirupanarruppatai
  • Perumpanarruppatai
  • Mullaippattu
  • Maduraikanchi
  • Nedunalvadai
  • Kurinjippattu
  • Pattinappalai
  • Malaipadukadam

The shortest work contains 103 lines, while the longest contains 782 lines.

Akam Works
  • Mullaippattu
  • Kurinjippattu
  • Nedunalvadai
  • Pattinappalai
Puram Works
  • Tirumurukarruppatai
  • Porunararruppatai
  • Sirupanarruppatai
  • Perumpanarruppatai
  • Malaipadukadam
  • Maduraikanchi

Five of the Puram works belong to the Arruppadai genre.

Arruppadai

Arruppadai means guiding or directing.

A performer who had received gifts from a patron guided another performer towards the same patron.

The five Arruppadai works in Pattuppattu are:

  • Tirumurukarruppatai
  • Porunararruppatai
  • Sirupanarruppatai
  • Perumpanarruppatai
  • Malaipadukadam or Koothararruppatai

Tirumurukarruppatai differs from the others because it guides a devotee towards Murugan rather than a performer towards a human patron.

Tirumurukarruppatai

Author: Nakkirar

Lines: 317

Other name: Pulavararruppatai

Subject: Murugan and his sacred places

A devotee who has received Murugan’s grace guides another seeker towards the deity.

The poem describes:

  • Tirupparankunram
  • Tiruchendur
  • Tiruvavinankudi or Palani
  • Erakam, traditionally associated with Swamimalai
  • Hill shrines
  • Pazhamudircholai
  • Murugan’s six faces and twelve arms
  • Worship by Kuravars and ascetics

It is placed at the beginning of Pattuppattu and functions like an invocation to the collection.

The identification of its Nakkirar with the author of Nedunalvadai remains debated.

Porunararruppatai

Author: Mudathamak Kanniyar

Patron: Karikala Chola

Lines: 248

A Porunan who had received gifts directs another performer to Karikala Chola.

The work describes:

  • Karikala’s patronage
  • Yal and musical performance
  • Viraliyar
  • Gifts of clothes, food, elephants, horses and chariots
  • Agricultural prosperity
  • Exchange of goods between ecological regions

The author, Mudathamak Kanniyar, was a woman poet.

Sirupanarruppatai

Author: Idaikkazhinattu Nallur Naththathanar

Patron: Oyman Nattu Nalliyakkodan

Lines: 269

Performer: Sirupanar, player of the small Yal

The work contains references to:

  • Nalliyakkodan
  • Oymanadu
  • Amur
  • Velur
  • Kidangil
  • Kadaiyezhu Vallalgal
  • Poverty of wandering performers
  • Siriyal or small Yal

It provides a compact literary account of the seven celebrated patrons.

Perumpanarruppatai

Author: Kadiyalur Uruthirankannanar

Patron: Tondaiman Ilanthiraiyan

Lines: 500

Performer: Perumpanar, player of the large Yal

The poem describes:

  • Kanchi
  • Tondaiman Ilanthiraiyan
  • Five ecological regions
  • Salt merchants
  • Caravan traders
  • Lighthouse
  • Tiruvekka temple
  • Periyal or large Yal
  • Hospitality along the route

Kadiyalur Uruthirankannanar also composed Pattinappalai.

Mullaippattu

Author: Kavirippumpattinathu Ponvanikanar Maganar Napputhanar

Lines: 103

Thinai: Mullai

Position: Shortest work in Pattuppattu

The heroine waits for the hero who has gone to war and promised to return during the rainy season.

The poem contains references to:

  • Military camp
  • Women carrying swords in the camp
  • Yavana guards
  • Pavai lamps
  • Time measurement using the Kannal instrument
  • Rainy-season landscape

Mullaippattu is the shortest of the Ten Long Poems.

Maduraikanchi

Author: Mangudi Maruthanar

Patron: Pandyan Nedunchezhiyan, victor of Talaiyalanganam

Lines: 782

Thinai: Kanchi

Position: Longest work in Pattuppattu

The poet advises the king about the impermanence of life and power.

The work describes:

  • Madurai city
  • Markets
  • Fortifications
  • Royal court
  • Festivals
  • Educational institutions
  • Religious establishments
  • Merchants and artisans
  • Day and night life of the city

Maduraikanchi is the longest of the Pattuppattu works.

Nedunalvadai

Author: Madurai Kanakkayanar Maganar Nakkirar

Lines: 188

Theme: Separation during the cold season

The cold northern wind appears long and painful to the queen but beneficial to the king engaged in military duty.

The poem describes:

  • Palace architecture
  • Queen’s chamber
  • Military camp
  • Wounded soldiers
  • Horses and elephants
  • Pavai lamps
  • Water outlets in the palace
  • Winter conditions

Some scholars classify it as Akam because it deals with separation. Others note its Puram elements because royal and military details make the ruler identifiable.

Kurinjippattu

Author: Kapilar

Lines: 261

Other name: Perunkurinji

Thinai: Kurinji

Tradition states that Kapilar composed it to explain Tamil Akam conventions to the Aryan king Prakatan.

The work is associated with:

  • Union of lovers
  • Arathodu Nittral
  • Mountain landscape
  • Kurinji communities
  • Description of 99 flowers

Kurinjippattu’s list of 99 flowers is one of its most frequently tested factual features.

Pattinappalai

Author: Kadiyalur Uruthirankannanar

Patron: Karikala Chola or Thirumavalavan

Lines: 301

Other name: Vanchi Nedumpattu

Thinai: Palai

Although its Akam framework concerns separation, most of the poem describes:

  • Kaveripoompattinam or Puhar
  • Port administration
  • Imports and exports
  • Warehouses
  • Customs officers
  • Tiger emblem stamped on goods
  • Foreign merchants
  • Karikala Chola
  • Cauvery and Chola prosperity

Kadiyalur Uruthirankannanar also wrote Perumpanarruppatai.

Malaipadukadam

Author: Iraniyamuttathu Perunkunrur Perunkausikanar

Patron: Nannan Sey Nannan

Lines: 583

Other name: Koothararruppatai

A rewarded performer guides another Koothar towards Nannan.

The title compares:

  • Mountain — elephant
  • Sounds arising from the mountain — the elephant’s flowing rut-fluid or Kadam

The poem describes:

  • Mountain routes
  • Nannan’s territory
  • Food and hospitality
  • Kuravar communities
  • Seyaru river
  • Musical instruments
  • Dangers faced by travellers

Musical instruments mentioned include:

  • Akuli
  • Pandil
  • Kodu
  • Kuzhal
  • Tattai
  • Ellari
  • Pathalai
  • Periyal
Major Sangam Poets

Poet–patron, poet–work and poet–Thinai associations are among the most frequently tested Sangam literary facts.

Kapilar

Kapilar is associated with:

  • Vel Pari
  • Pari’s daughters Angavai and Sangavai
  • Kurinjippattu
  • Kurinji section of Ainkurunuru
  • Kurinjikkali in Kalithokai
  • Seventh decad of Pathitrupathu on Selvak Kadungo Vazhiyathan
  • Numerous Akananuru, Natrinai, Kuruntokai and Purananuru poems

He was particularly celebrated for Kurinji poetry.

Avvaiyar

The Sangam-period Avvaiyar is associated with:

  • Adiyaman Neduman Anji
  • Gooseberry tradition
  • Diplomatic mission to Tondaiman
  • Poems in Purananuru
  • Poems in Akananuru, Kuruntokai and Natrinai

The Sangam Avvaiyar must not be confused with later medieval poets who also used the name Avvaiyar.

Nakkirar

Nakkirar is traditionally associated with:

  • Tirumurukarruppatai
  • Nedunalvadai
  • Pandyan court
  • Commentary tradition linked with Iraiyanar Akapporul

Whether the authors of Tirumurukarruppatai and Nedunalvadai were the same Nakkirar remains debated.

Paranar

Paranar composed poems on several rulers and chiefs.

He is especially associated with:

  • Fifth decad of Pathitrupathu
  • Cheran Senguttuvan
  • Poems in Purananuru
  • Poems in Akananuru
  • Historical and battle references
Kaniyan Pungundranar

Kaniyan Pungundranar composed Purananuru 192.

Its opening words are:

Yadhum Oore Yaavarum Kelir

It expresses a universal outlook in which every place is regarded as one’s town and all people as relatives.

Bharatham Paadiya Perunthevanar

Perunthevanar is known by the title Bharatham Paadiya, meaning one who sang or translated the Bharata tradition.

He composed invocatory verses for several anthologies, including:

  • Natrinai
  • Kuruntokai
  • Ainkurunuru
  • Akananuru
  • Purananuru

The invocations praise different deities, including Thirumal, Murugan and Siva.

Women Poets

Important Sangam women poets include:

  • Avvaiyar
  • Mudathamak Kanniyar
  • Kakkaipadiniyar Nachellaiyar
  • Okkur Masathiyar
  • Vellivithiyar
  • Allur Nanmullaiyar
  • Ponmudiyar
  • Aathimandiyar

Kakkaipadiniyar Nachellaiyar composed the sixth decad of Pathitrupathu.

Mudathamak Kanniyar composed Porunararruppatai.

Other Major Poets
  • Kaniyan Pungundranar — Purananuru 192 and the universal statement “Yadhum Oore Yaavarum Kelir”.
  • Pisirandaiyar — remembered for friendship with Kopperuncholan.
  • Kovur Kilar — advised Chola rulers and intervened during political conflict.
  • Mangudi Maruthanar — author of Maduraikanchi.
  • Kadiyalur Uruthirankannanar — author of Perumpanarruppatai and Pattinappalai.
  • Idaikkazhinattu Nallur Naththathanar — author of Sirupanarruppatai.
  • Perunkunrur Perunkausikanar — author of Malaipadukadam.
  • Kudalur Kilar — compiler of Ainkurunuru.
  • Nallanthuvanar — compiler of Kalithokai and author of its Neithal section.
Metres and Literary Techniques

Sangam works use characteristic metres and indirect techniques that shape how emotion and narrative are expressed.

Important Metres
Akaval or Asiriyappa

The dominant metre of much Sangam poetry.

Used extensively in:

  • Purananuru
  • Akananuru
  • Natrinai
  • Kuruntokai
  • Pattuppattu works
Kalippa

Used in Kalithokai.

Paripadal

Both the name of a metre and the anthology composed in that form.

Vanchippa

Appears prominently within Pattinappalai, which is also known as Vanchi Nedumpattu.

Important Literary Techniques
Antati

The final word, syllable or idea of one poem connects with the beginning of the next; the fourth decad of Pathitrupathu and the Tondippattu section of Ainkurunuru use this pattern.

Dialogue and Dramatic Presentation

Kalithokai frequently presents emotional situations through dialogue and dramatic movement.

Indirect Expression

Ullurai and Iraichi allow landscape, animals and natural objects to suggest human emotions without direct statement.

Ullurai

An implied comparison in which the natural scene indirectly expresses human emotion.

Iraichi

An indirect or suggestive meaning conveyed through the behaviour of animals, birds or natural objects.

Uvamai

Simile or explicit comparison.

Historical Evidence, Limitations and Recovery

Sangam works preserve historical information, but praise, convention and textual loss require comparison with other evidence and careful editorial recovery.

Work–Information Associations
  • Pathitrupathu — Chera rulers and genealogy
  • Pattinappalai — Puhar and Chola maritime trade
  • Maduraikanchi — Madurai city and Pandya administration
  • Perumpanarruppatai — Kanchi and Tondaiman Ilanthiraiyan
  • Porunararruppatai — Karikala Chola and bardic patronage
  • Sirupanarruppatai — Kadaiyezhu Vallalgal and Nalliyakkodan
  • Purananuru — kings, chiefs, wars, ethics and heroism
  • Akananuru — love poetry with historical references
  • Paripadal — music, Murugan, Thirumal, Madurai and Vaigai
  • Kurinjippattu — Kurinji landscape and 99 flowers
  • Malaipadukadam — hill routes, Nannan and musical instruments
Literary Evidence Must Be Used Carefully

Sangam poems contain:

  • Historical names
  • Real places
  • Battles
  • Trade references
  • Social customs
  • Poetic conventions
  • Praise and exaggeration

A literary title such as Imayavaramban or a poetic account of universal conquest should not automatically be treated as proof of permanent political control.

Sangam literature should be compared with inscriptions, archaeology, coins and foreign accounts.

Recovery of Sangam Works

Many Sangam texts survived through palm-leaf manuscripts and quotations in later commentaries.

U. V. Swaminatha Iyer, popularly known as Tamil Thatha, collected manuscripts, compared different copies and published several classical works.

He published Pattuppattu in print in 1889.

His work was central to the modern recovery of Purananuru, Pathitrupathu, Ainkurunuru and other early Tamil texts.

C. W. Damodaram Pillai

He was an early editor of palm-leaf manuscripts and printed critical editions of ancient Tamil works, including Tolkappiyam and Kalithokai. His work preceded and complemented the later publication activity of U. V. Swaminatha Iyer.

Rapid Revision and High-Yield Distinctions

This final topic consolidates work–author, work–patron, poem count, metre, alternate name, missing portion and common distinction facts.

Rapid Revision
Main Classification
  • Tolkappiyam — grammar and poetics
  • Ettuthokai — eight anthologies
  • Pattuppattu — ten long poems
  • Ettuthokai + Pattuppattu — Pathinenmelkanakku
Three Sangams — Traditional Account
  • First — Then Madurai
  • Second — Kapatapuram
  • Third — Madurai
  • Main source — commentary on Iraiyanar Akapporul
Tolkappiyam
  • Author — Tolkappiyar
  • Divisions — Ezhuthu, Sol and Porul
  • Nine Iyals in each division
  • Akam and Puram systematised in Poruladikaram
Ettuthokai — Akam
  • Natrinai — 400 medium-length poems
  • Kuruntokai — 400 short poems — Purikko
  • Ainkurunuru — 500 poems — five poets
  • Akananuru — 400 long Akam poems — Nedunthokai
  • Kalithokai — 150 poems — Kalippa
Ettuthokai — Puram
  • Purananuru — 400 Puram poems
  • Pathitrupathu — Chera rulers — 80 surviving poems
Mixed Collection
  • Paripadal — devotion, music, Vaigai, Murugan and Thirumal
Ainkurunuru Authors
  • Marutham — Orampogiyar
  • Neithal — Ammuvanar
  • Kurinji — Kapilar
  • Palai — Othalant aiyar
  • Mullai — Peyanar
Akananuru Divisions
  • Kalittriyanai Nirai — 1–120
  • Manimidai Pavalam — 121–300
  • Nittilakkovai — 301–400
Pattuppattu Authors and Patrons
  • Tirumurukarruppatai — Nakkirar — Murugan
  • Porunararruppatai — Mudathamak Kanniyar — Karikala
  • Sirupanarruppatai — Nallur Naththathanar — Nalliyakkodan
  • Perumpanarruppatai — Uruthirankannanar — Ilanthiraiyan
  • Mullaippattu — Napputhanar
  • Maduraikanchi — Mangudi Maruthanar — Nedunchezhiyan
  • Nedunalvadai — Nakkirar
  • Kurinjippattu — Kapilar
  • Pattinappalai — Uruthirankannanar — Karikala
  • Malaipadukadam — Perunkausikanar — Nannan
Important Numerical Facts
  • Mullaippattu — 103 lines — shortest Pattuppattu work
  • Maduraikanchi — 782 lines — longest Pattuppattu work
  • Kurinjippattu — 99 flowers
  • Pathitrupathu — first and tenth decads lost
  • Paripadal — originally 70; 22 complete poems survive
  • Kalithokai — 150 poems
  • Ainkurunuru — five groups of 100 poems
High-Yield Distinctions
  • Pathitrupathu concerns Chera rulers; Purananuru concerns several rulers and chiefs.
  • Akananuru is also called Nedunthokai.
  • Malaipadukadam is also called Koothararruppatai.
  • Tirumurukarruppatai guides a devotee to Murugan; the other Arruppadai works guide performers to patrons.
  • Paripadal records the poet, musical composer and Pann.
  • Kalithokai is written in Kalippa and contains dramatic dialogues.
  • Kurinjippattu contains the famous description of 99 flowers.
  • Mullaippattu is the shortest Pattuppattu work.
  • Maduraikanchi is the longest Pattuppattu work.
  • Pattinappalai describes Puhar, despite belonging to the Palai Akam framework.
  • Kadiyalur Uruthirankannanar wrote both Perumpanarruppatai and Pattinappalai.
  • Kapilar composed Kurinjippattu and the Kurinji section of Ainkurunuru.
  • Mudathamak Kanniyar, author of Porunararruppatai, was a woman poet.
  • Sangam Avvaiyar must not be confused with later Avvaiyars.
  • The story of three Sangams is a later literary tradition, not a securely established chronology.
  • Ettuthokai and Pattuppattu Ettuthokai contains eight anthologies; Pattuppattu contains ten long poems.
  • Akam and Puram Akam concerns private emotional life, while Puram concerns public action and named historical actors.
  • Kaikkilai and Perunthinai Kaikkilai is one-sided love; Perunthinai is unsuitable or mismatched love.
  • Akananuru and Purananuru Akananuru is an Akam anthology; Purananuru is a Puram anthology.
  • Literary and inscriptional evidence A poem may preserve names and events but must be tested against inscriptions, archaeology, coins and foreign accounts.
  • Nakkirar authorship The identification of the authors of Tirumurukarruppatai and Nedunalvadai as the same Nakkirar remains debated.
